stem: Which pillar of OOP consists in wrapping data and the functions that work on it together into a single unit, the class?
explanation: Encapsulation bundles the data (attributes) and the functions that operate on it (methods) into one unit: the class.

distractor_notes.a: Abstraction means exposing only the essential features of an object and hiding the irrelevant details.
distractor_notes.c: Inheritance is a subclass acquiring the members of another class.
distractor_notes.d: Polymorphism is objects having their own behaviour while sharing the interface of their parent class.

stem: Showing only the essential features of an object to the outside world and hiding the irrelevant information is called:
explanation: Abstraction is about the outside view of an object: only the necessary features are shown, the rest is hidden.

distractor_notes.a: Encapsulation is bundling data and functions into a class; abstraction is about what is exposed to the outside.
distractor_notes.b: Polymorphism is the same interface with different behaviours.
distractor_notes.d: Instantiation is creating an object from a class; it is not one of the 4 pillars.

stem: Classes `Cat` and `Fish` both inherit from `Animal` and each redefines the method `move()`. A loop calls `a.move()` on every element of a mixed list of animals, and the same call produces a different behaviour depending on the object's class. Which OOP concept does this illustrate?
explanation: Polymorphism: one call (`a.move()`), many behaviours, chosen by the class of the object. Overriding a parent method in child classes is exactly what the course calls polymorphism.

distractor_notes.a: Encapsulation is bundling data and methods in a class, not choosing behaviour per object.
distractor_notes.b: Abstraction is hiding irrelevant details from the outside.
distractor_notes.d: Instantiation is creating objects, not the varying behaviour of one call.

verify.reference: Slides 187 (4 pillars) and 194 (overriding methods is polymorphism)

stem: Which expressions evaluate to True? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Built-in types are classes: [] is an instance of list, 'abc' of str, and every value (even 3) is an object. `dir(list)` lists the members of the class, including `append`. The class list itself is an instance of `type` (so `type(list) is type`), and `type()` returns a class, not a string.

distractor_notes.c: list is a class; the type of a class is `type`.
distractor_notes.f: `type(5)` is the class int, not the string 'int'.

stem: Given the code, which expressions run without raising an error? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: A single leading underscore (`_code`) is only a convention meaning 'internal': access still works. Two leading underscores trigger name mangling: inside the class `__key` is stored as `_Safe__key`, so `s.__key` from outside raises AttributeError, while the class's own methods and the mangled name still reach it. Python encapsulation relies on conventions, not on strict privacy.

distractor_notes.b: Outside the class the name is not mangled, and no attribute literally named `__key` exists → AttributeError.

stem: What is the output of the following code?
explanation: Inside the class, `self.__key` is mangled into `self._Safe__key`. Outside the class no mangling happens, so `s.__key = 'xyz'` creates a different attribute literally named `__key`. `reveal()` still reads `_Safe__key` → 'abc', and `s.__key` now exists → 'xyz'.

distractor_notes.a: The outside assignment does not touch the mangled attribute `_Safe__key`.
distractor_notes.d: After the assignment, an attribute named `__key` exists on s.
distractor_notes.b: `s.__key` reads the new attribute created outside the class.

stem: Given the function, which calls return 10? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: `*args` collects all the positional arguments into a tuple; the parameters after it (`verbose`, `start`) are keyword-only and can only be set by name. `total(5, 5, 10)` sums all three (20): 10 does not go into start. Passing a list gives `args = ([1, 2, 3, 4],)` and `0 + list` fails, while `*[...]` unpacks it into 4 separate arguments.

distractor_notes.c: The list is one single argument: `0 + [1, 2, 3, 4]` raises TypeError.
distractor_notes.e: 10 is also collected in args (sum 20); start can only be given as `start=10`.

stem: What happens in the below code?
explanation: `factor` comes after `*values`, so it is a keyword-only parameter, and it has no default. All the positional arguments go into values and factor is never given: TypeError (missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'factor'). Call it as `scale(1, 2, 3, factor=2)`.

distractor_notes.b: Python never uses the last positional argument for a keyword-only parameter.
distractor_notes.c: factor has no default value of 1.

stem: What is the output of the following code?
explanation: `*args` collects the extra positional arguments into a tuple (1, 2), and `**kwargs` collects the keyword arguments into a dict {'a': 3}.

distractor_notes.b: args is a tuple, not a list.
distractor_notes.c: `a=3` is a keyword argument, so it goes into kwargs.
distractor_notes.a: kwargs is a dict and args a tuple.

stem: What will be the output of the code?
explanation: The `def` rebinds the name `sum`, hiding the built-in function. The new sum receives a single argument, the list, so `args = ([1, 2, 3],)` and the loop computes `0 + [1, 2, 3]` → TypeError. The built-in would give 6; this version expects `sum(1, 2, 3)`. Avoid reusing built-in names.

distractor_notes.a: The built-in sum is shadowed by the new definition.
distractor_notes.b: `0 + list` fails instead of producing the list.
distractor_notes.d: The loop body runs once (with the list) and fails.

stem: What is the output of the following code?
explanation: item takes 'tea'; every other positional argument goes into the tuple extras, including 'L', because size comes after `*extras` and is keyword-only, so it keeps 'M'. The unknown keyword `sugar=2` goes into the dict notes.

distractor_notes.a: A keyword-only parameter is never filled by a positional argument.
distractor_notes.c: extras is a tuple, not a list.

stem: What happens in the below code?
explanation: Positional arguments are bound first: 1 goes to a and 2 into args. Then `a=3` tries to bind a a second time → TypeError (got multiple values for argument 'a'). `**kwargs` only collects keywords that do not match a named parameter.

distractor_notes.b: A keyword argument does not override a positional one; they conflict.
distractor_notes.c: The call fails before the function body runs.

stem: Given the function, which calls run without a TypeError? (Select all that apply.)
code:
def g(a, b=2, *args, c, **kw):
    return a
explanation: a is required, b has a default, extra positional arguments go into args, c is keyword-only and required (no default), and unknown keywords go into kw. `g(1, 2, 3)` never supplies c, and `g(1, 2, c=3, b=4)` gives b twice (by position and by keyword).

distractor_notes.b: c is keyword-only and required: 3 goes into args → TypeError (missing keyword-only argument 'c').
distractor_notes.e: b receives 2 by position and 4 by keyword → TypeError (multiple values for 'b').

stem: What will be the output of the code?
code:
def foo(*args, **kwargs):
    print(args)
    print(kwargs)

words = ['one', 'two']
foo(words)
explanation: Without `*`, the list is passed as one single argument, so args is a tuple containing the list: the program prints `(['one', 'two'],)` and then `{}` (no keyword arguments gives an empty dict). None of the listed outputs matches. `foo(*words)` would unpack the list and print ('one', 'two').

distractor_notes.a: That is the output of `foo(*words)`; without `*` the list is not unpacked.
distractor_notes.b: args is always a tuple, even with a single argument: here a tuple containing the list.
distractor_notes.c: kwargs is an empty dict, never None (and the list was not unpacked).

stem: In the MVC pattern, which component holds the data and its related logic?
explanation: Model = the data and the logic attached to it; View = presentation and user interaction; Controller = the interface between Model and View.

distractor_notes.b: The View presents data to the user and handles user interaction.
distractor_notes.c: The Controller is the interface between Model and View.
distractor_notes.d: Router is not one of the three MVC components.

stem: In a 3-tier architecture, which tier coordinates the application, processes commands, makes logical decisions and performs calculations?
explanation: The logic (application) tier sits in the middle: it processes commands, makes decisions and calculations, and moves data between the presentation tier (user interface) and the data tier (database / file storage).

distractor_notes.a: The presentation tier is the user interface: it translates tasks and results for the user.
distractor_notes.c: The data tier stores and retrieves information from a database or file system.
distractor_notes.d: There is no network tier among the 3 tiers.

stem: This mini `Button` class mimics a Tk button. What is the output of the code?
explanation: `command=say_hi()` calls the function immediately, while the arguments are built: 'hi' is printed at creation and command receives the return value, None. `click()` then does nothing. To register a callback, pass the function itself: `command=say_hi` (or a lambda).

distractor_notes.a: That is what `command=say_hi` (without parentheses) would print.
distractor_notes.c: say_hi ran once, at creation; the stored command is None.
distractor_notes.b: `click` tests `if self.command`, so a None command is silently skipped.

stem: These lambdas could be the `command` callbacks of three buttons created in a loop. What is the output of the code?
explanation: A lambda captures the variable i, not its value at creation time: the value is looked up when the lambda is called. By then the loop is over and i is 2. The usual fix is `lambda i=i: print(i)`, since a default value is evaluated at creation.

distractor_notes.a: That is the behaviour of `lambda i=i: print(i)`.
distractor_notes.d: i still exists after the loop (a for loop has no block scope).
distractor_notes.b: The lookup happens at call time and finds the last value of i.

stem: Which Tkinter widget is meant for single-line text input?
explanation: Entry is the single-line input field; Text is the multi-line text widget, Label displays text, Canvas draws vector and pixel graphics.

distractor_notes.b: A Label only displays text; the user cannot type in it.
distractor_notes.c: Text is the multi-line text widget.
distractor_notes.d: Canvas is for drawing (vector and pixel graphics).

stem: With these definitions, which expressions can be passed as `command=` to a Tk button so that something is appended to `calls` **only when the button is clicked** (Tk calls the command with no argument)? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Tk needs a callable that it will call later with no argument: a function name (`save`), a lambda wrapping a call that needs arguments, or a callable object (an instance of a class with `__call__`). `save()` and `save_as('x')` run immediately when the button is created and pass their result, None. `Saver` is the class: calling it only builds a new object and records nothing.

distractor_notes.b: The parentheses call save immediately; command receives None.
distractor_notes.d: Called at creation and returns None; wrap it in a lambda instead.
distractor_notes.f: Calling the class creates an instance; `__call__` is not executed.
